newsitem.title: CHINA: China says imports to reach $149 billion in 1996.
newsitem.headline: China says imports to reach $149 billion in 1996.

text.p: China's imports are expected to gather momentum in the months ahead and reach $149 billion for the full year, up 13 percent over 1995, the Business Weekly said on Sunday.

Increased imports of capital equipment should show up in fourth quarter statistics, reflecting two rounds of domestic interest rate cuts in recent months, the newspaper quoted Zhu Baoliang of the State Information Centre as saying.
He said that efforts to stimulate exports would also encourage companies to bring in capital goods for production of items that would be aimed at overseas markets.
The newspaper did not give any forecast for exports or the overall trade balance.
China said recently that it expected a trade surplus of $2.9 billion this year, down sharply from the surplus of $16.7 billion in 1995.
China's imports were up 9.9 percent year-on-year to $74.47 billion in the January-July period.
The newspaper quoted Zhu as saying that the growth in imports in recent months was surprisingly weak despite a reduction in tariff rates as of April 1.
One of the factors contributing to that slow rise in imports despite the tariff cuts was the reduction in the number of goods given duty-free treatment.
Duty-free treatment for products imported under barter trade was abolished this year, and this has led to a drop in imports of these items.

Tighter controls on what is known as the import processing trade has also been a factor. Processing, where materials are imported for use in light industry and then re-exported, is common in sectors such as toys, textiles and leather goods.
Zhu said that in the past, processing materials, which are imported duty-free and are supposed to be re-exported, had often found their way onto the domestic market.
